clinicalPearls: Characterised by ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves with sensory loss in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
A fixed dilated pupil and ptosis may be present from third nerve involvement, and sympathetic fibres passing through can also be affected
Vision is characteristically spared because the optic nerve exits through the separate optic canal, not the fissure
Progression to include the optic nerve signals extension to the orbital apex (orbital apex syndrome)
The syndrome may follow trauma with fractures involving the fissure, or result from tumour or inflammation
Periorbital pain, proptosis, and reduced corneal sensation are common accompanying features
Careful assessment of vision distinguishes this from orbital apex syndrome and guides urgency
reference.pathophysiology: The superior orbital fissure is the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid that transmits the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves, the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, sympathetic fibres, and the superior ophthalmic vein. A lesion here compresses or infiltrates these structures to produce ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, a dilated pupil, and forehead sensory loss, while the optic nerve is spared because it passes through the adjacent optic canal. Causes include trauma, tumour, granulomatous inflammation, infection, and vascular lesions in the region.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital apex syndrome with added optic neuropathy
Thyroid eye disease with restrictive ophthalmoplegia
Multiple ocular motor nerve palsies from other skull base pathology
additionalInvestigations: CT of the orbit and skull base, particularly after trauma, to assess the fissure and fractures
MRI of the orbit and cavernous sinus with contrast
Assessment of visual acuity and the afferent pupillary pathway to exclude apex involvement
Screening for tumour or metastatic disease where relevant
Trigeminal sensory testing to map the deficit
redFlags: Any decline in vision indicating extension to the orbital apex
Signs of orbital infection needing urgent treatment
A history of significant trauma with orbital fracture
Rapidly progressive cranial neuropathies suggesting tumour or aggressive inflammation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; traumatic and inflammatory cases may recover partially or fully with appropriate management, whereas neoplastic causes are more guarded, and some ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss can persist.
pitfalls: Failing to check vision and thereby missing progression to orbital apex syndrome
Confusing it with cavernous sinus syndrome, which more often involves the maxillary trigeminal division and can cause a Horner syndrome
Overlooking a treatable inflammatory or infective cause
Attributing all findings to trauma without imaging the fissure
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, using corticosteroids for granulomatous or inflammatory disease, antimicrobials for infection and oncological therapy for tumour
Undertake urgent surgical decompression when trauma with a fracture or haematoma compresses the fissure and produces a progressive deficit
Protect the cornea with lubricants and lid taping where corneal sensation is reduced, to prevent exposure keratopathy
Monitor visual acuity and the afferent pupillary response to detect extension to the orbital apex
Refer for combined neurosurgery, ophthalmology, oncology and maxillofacial input according to the aetiology
